Accept path (SVG path data) in node.set for vectors, with the same width/height scaling rules as node.create, keeping the layer's id, paints, effects and bindings.

→ {"families": [{"family": "SF Pro", "layers": 1}]}. "System Font" renders as SF Pro.

On macOS, resolve SF Pro, SF Pro Text and SF Pro Display (and maybe .SF NS, -apple-system) to the system font when no separately installed SF Pro family exists. Keep "System Font" as the canonical name if you prefer. A .fig import of an iOS design that uses "SF Pro" would then render without substitution.

Recreating an iOS app, the first thing an agent does is set fontFamily: "SF Pro". Finding out that it's called "System Font" takes a probe-and-check round trip.

#998 Attached MCP: let each call name the document it targets, instead of acting on the tab in front

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-21 by kkilchrist · updated 2026-10-21

Summary

With figcraft-cli mcp --attach, every tool call acts on whichever document tab is in front. If the user switches tabs while an agent is working, or two agents share the app (one per open file), the agent's next edit lands in the wrong document. Nothing in the call or the result guards against it.

This happened in practice: while one agent session was editing a design file through the attached app, a second session opened a different project's file in the same window. Every call from the first agent then depended on which tab happened to be in front. The workaround is to do all editing headless and attach only to open the result, which works, but makes attached mode unsafe for the "watch the agent design" workflow docs/mcp.md describes.

Proposal

  1. An optional document parameter on every tool and command, by path or tab index: 
    {"name":"batch","arguments":{"document":"/path/to/design.figcraft","commands":[…]}}
    The call acts on that document whether or not it's in front, or fails with a clear error if it isn't open.
  2. Every mutating result includes the document it changed (path and name), so a client can verify it.
  3. Optionally, --attach 7979 --document PATH pins a whole MCP session to one file.

Environment

figcraft-cli 0.8.0 / FigCraft 0.8.0 (macOS universal), macOS 27.2, figcraft-cli mcp --attach 7979.

Proposed shape, now that #1003–#1007 are up. It mirrors what the control protocol already does for windows: "any method takes window (an id from window.list) to run in that window; without it, requests go to the window last in front".

A document param alongside window

  • Any control method or MCP tool takes an optional document: an open file's path, or a tab uid (DocState::uid), listed by a small document.list or added to window.list / ui.inspect. The request runs on that document. Without document, behaviour is exactly as today.
  • The user's visible tab doesn't change. The engine switches Session::active for the request and restores it afterwards, the same save-and-restore of active that Session::grouped does. If the document isn't open, the call fails with a clear error.
  • Changing results name the document they acted on ("document": {"uid", "path", "name"}), so a client can verify.
  • MCP: every tool gets an optional document argument. figcraft-cli mcp --attach PORT --document PATH pins a whole session to one file and fails clearly if it isn't open.

  3. Where should the switch live: in the control dispatch (control.rs, next to the window handling), or as a Session helper the CLI and MCP backends can share?

#997 open_file returns the stale open copy when the file has changed on disk (no reload or revert)

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-21 by kkilchrist · updated 2026-10-21

Summary

open_file on a path that's already open returns that tab ("index"), even when the file on disk is newer. Nothing in the result says the copy is stale. The only way to see the new contents is file.close followed by open_file, which also throws away undo history and refuses (or needs force) if the tab has unsaved changes.

This comes up whenever two processes touch one file. A natural agent workflow does exactly that: build in headless figcraft-cli mcp (safe from tab switches), save_file, then open_file the path in the attached app so the user can see it. If the app already had the file open, the user keeps looking at the old version.

Steps to reproduce (one headless session)

  1. run_command node.create {type: frame, name: "Original"} → id 2
  2. save_file {path: F}
  3. Outside the server: figcraft-cli run rename.json --in F --out F, where rename.json = [{"command":"node.set","params":{"ids":[2],"props":{"name":"ChangedOnDisk"}}}]
  4. open_file {path: F} → "index": 0, "dirty": false
  5. get_node {id: 2} → name Original
  6. file.close, then open_file {path: F}, then get_node {id: 2} → ChangedOnDisk

Proposal

  • open_file {path, reload: true} (or a file.revert command) that rereads the file into the open tab when it's clean, and errors with a clear message when it has unsaved changes.
  • Without reload, include "stale": true in the result when the file on disk is newer than the open copy.

Environment

figcraft-cli 0.8.0 (macOS universal), macOS 27.2. Seen headless and with mcp --attach.

#995 edit.duplicate: return which copy is which (an id map for duplicated descendants)

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-21 by kkilchrist · updated 2026-10-21

Summary

edit.duplicate returns the ids of the top-level copies only. To edit something inside a copy (a label in a duplicated screen, a nested instance), a caller has to inspect the whole copied tree and match layers by name and position, or guess ids by offset. Guessing by offset works until instance swaps or reparenting change the id order, and then edits silently land on the wrong layers.

Steps to reproduce

[{"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"frame","name":"Card"}},
 {"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"text","name":"Title","text":"t","parent":2}},
 {"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"text","name":"Detail","text":"d","parent":2}},
 {"command":"edit.duplicate","params":{"ids":[2]}}]

→ {"ids": [5]}. Nothing says which new ids are the copies of Title (#3) and Detail (#4).

Proposal

An opt-in map, so default results stay small:

{"command":"edit.duplicate","params":{"ids":[2],"map":true}}
→ {"ids":[5], "map": {"2":5, "3":6, "4":7}}

Combined with step-reference paths (separate issue), a batch could then edit inside the copy: {"$step": 3, "field": "map.3"}. The same map would help page.duplicate and edit.paste.

Why it matters

A common agent workflow is "duplicate the light screens, switch the copies to the Dark variable mode, then fix a few layers in the copies". Today the third step needs a large inspection call per screen (see #912 for how large those get).

Environment

figcraft-cli 0.8.0 (macOS universal), macOS 27.2.

Found by Claude (Opus 5.5) in Claude Code while building about 80 phone screens through the FigCraft MCP server. Repro verified on 0.8.0 before filing.

map: true on the commands that copy layers

{"command": "edit.duplicate", "params": {"ids": [2], "map": true}}
→ {"ids": [8], "map": {"2": 8, "3": 9, "4": 10}}
  • map pairs every original layer, descendants included, with its copy. It's opt-in, so default results stay as small as today.
  • It follows the pattern page.duplicate already uses internally: doc.subtree(original) zipped with doc.subtree(copy), which works because copy_in_file and duplicate_all_into keep the structure and order. page.duplicate already builds this list for its flows, so it could return it with map: true too.
  • edit.paste would be the third user. Its copies go through the clipboard (adopt_pasted already has a BTreeMap<NodeId, NodeId>), so its map would pair the copied source layers with the pasted ones.
  • With #1003, a batch can then edit inside a copy without inspecting it: {"$ref": "copy", "field": "map/3"} is the copy of layer 3.

  1. Map keys are strings because JSON object keys have to be. Is that fine, or would you prefer a list of [original, copy] pairs?
  2. Should map include instance sublayers? They're re-synced from their main, but their ids are still stable targets for overrides.

#994 command.batch: named step references and paths into results (e.g. the ids from edit.duplicate)

maintainer labelmultiple issues · opened 2026-10-21 by kkilchrist · updated 2026-10-21

Summary

Step references are positional: {"$step": n}. In long batches (30–60 steps, which is common when an agent builds a screen in one undo step), counting step numbers by hand is the most frequent source of failed batches. Separately, field takes only a top-level key, so a result like edit.duplicate's {"ids": [5]} can't be referenced at all.

What happens today

[{"command":"command.batch","params":{"commands":[
 {"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"frame","name":"Original"}},
 {"command":"edit.duplicate","params":{"ids":[{"$step":0}]}},
 {"command":"node.set","params":{"ids":[{"$step":1,"field":"ids.0"}],"props":{"name":"Copy"}}}]}}]

→ invalid parameters for command.batch: step 2: step 1's result has no ids.0 (ids/0 fails the same way).

Proposal

  1. Named steps: an optional "as": "card" on a step, referenced with {"$ref": "card"} (and {"$ref": "card", "field": …}). Positional $step keeps working.
  2. Paths in field: "ids.0" (or a JSON Pointer such as "/ids/0") so array results can be used.

Evidence from use

In one working session, building about 80 screens with batches of 20–60 steps, six batches failed only because a later edit shifted the step numbers by one (an inserted step, or a text node counted twice). Each failure was caught and rolled back cleanly, which is great, but each cost a full resend. Named references would have avoided all six. The rollback and the error naming the failing step are excellent; this request builds on them.

Environment

figcraft-cli 0.8.0 (macOS universal), macOS 27.2, MCP headless and attached.

Steps to reproduce

[{"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"component","name":"Card","props":{"layout":"vertical"}}},

 {"command":"instance.create","params":{"component":2,"x":300}},
 {"command":"node.get","params":{"id":3,"depth":0}},
 {"command":"node.get","params":{"id":5,"depth":0}}]

Note (#3, in the main component) is hidden, matching the property's default, as in Figma, where a boolean property's value on the main is the layer's visibility.

  • Note #5 in the instance: visible: false
  • component.properties reports default: false

#992 node.reparent: index within the same parent counts slots before the move, so moving a layer down one place does nothing

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-21 by kkilchrist · updated 2026-10-21

Summary

node.reparent {ids, parent, index} with parent set to the layer's current parent reads index against the child list before the layer is taken out. Moving a layer from slot 0 to slot 1 is a no-op, and asking for slot 2 puts it in slot 1. Moving a layer up works as expected. The command reports ok: true in all cases, and the index semantics aren't documented ({ids?, parent, index?} in list_commands; docs/mcp.md only mentions node.reparent in passing).

Steps to reproduce

figcraft-cli run repro.json:

[{"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"frame","name":"Row","props":{"layout":"horizontal"}}},
 {"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"text","name":"first","text":"first","parent":2}},
 {"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"text","name":"second","text":"second","parent":2}},
 {"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"text","name":"third","text":"third","parent":2}},
 {"command":"node.reparent","params":{"ids":[3],"parent":2,"index":1}},
 {"command":"node.get","params":{"id":2,"depth":1}}]

Expected

Row children: second, first, third (first now at index 1).

Actual

Row children: first, second, third. Nothing moved, and the step returned {"ok": true}. With "index": 2 the result is second, first, third. Moving third to "index": 0 gives third, … as expected.

Why it matters

An agent reordering layers (for example, putting a chevron after a label in an auto layout row) gets ok back and has no signal that nothing happened. It only finds out from a screenshot.

Suggestion

Either treat index as the layer's final position (what arrange.reorder's "insert at target's visual slot" suggests), or document "insert before the child currently at index" in the command's parameter text. If nothing moves, returning {"ok": true, "moved": false} would also help.

Environment

figcraft-cli 0.8.0 (macOS universal), macOS 27.2. Also seen through figcraft-cli mcp (headless) and mcp --attach.

Found by Claude (Opus 5.5) in Claude Code while building about 80 phone screens through the FigCraft MCP server. Repro verified on 0.8.0 before filing.

#964 [Feature Request] Align to a key object when multiple elements are selected

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-21 by culiulemon · updated 2026-10-21

Summary

When aligning multiple selected elements, I'd like to choose which element acts as the alignment reference (the key object), instead of the alignment always being computed against the overall bounding box of the selection.

Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Currently, after selecting multiple elements, all alignment operations (align left / center / right / top / middle / bottom, and distribute) are calculated against the combined bounding box of the entire selection. This means:

  • I cannot align the rest of the selection to a specific element's edge or center — e.g. "align all other selected elements to the left edge of element A".
  • If element A itself is meant to stay fixed while the others move, I have to nudge the others manually or repeat the alignment after temporarily moving A, which is slow and imprecise.

This is a very common layout task: one element is the anchor, and everything else should snap to it.

Describe the solution you'd like

When multiple elements are selected, allow designating one of them as the key object (the reference that stays in place while the others align to it). Proposed interactions:

  • Click an already-selected element to set it as the key object (it could be highlighted with a thicker/different selection outline, as in Adobe Illustrator).
  • Once a key object is set, all existing align/distribute commands act against that object's bounds instead of the selection's overall bounds.
  • A way to clear the key object (e.g. click it again, or press Esc), falling back to normal selection-bounding-box alignment.

Example behavior: with elements A, B, C selected and A as the key object, pressing "Align left" moves B and C so their left edges match A's left edge, while A does not move.

Describe alternatives you've considered

  • Manually nudging each element to match the key object — imprecise and slow.
  • Using groups/constraints or laying the key object out first, then aligning the rest in smaller selections — extra steps and doesn't cover distributes.
  • Third-party plugins/scripts — works, but should be built-in for a core alignment workflow.

Additional context

This is standard behavior in tools like Adobe Illustrator ("key object" alignment) and is frequently requested in our team's daily layout work. It would make multi-element alignment far more flexible and accurate.

#960 macOS: opening a figcraft://join?… link activates the app but never joins the session

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-21 by afloury · updated 2026-10-21

What happens

On macOS, clicking a figcraft://join?host=…&file=…&token=… invite link (from a browser, or open "figcraft://join?…" in Terminal) brings FigCraft to the front, but no session is joined. This happens whether FigCraft is already running or not.

Pasting the same link into File › Join live session… joins fine, so the link itself is valid.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Publish a file to a figcraft-server and copy its edit link (figcraft://join?host=<host>:<port>&file=<id>&token=<token>).
  2. On macOS, run open "figcraft://join?host=…&file=…&token=…", or click the link in a web page.
  3. FigCraft activates, but no session tab opens.

Expected

The app joins the session, as it does when the link is passed on the command line (Linux %U), or pasted into Join live session.

Cause (from reading the 0.8.0 source, commit 594dc8c)

  • On macOS, LaunchServices does not put a URL in argv. It delivers it as a kInternetEventClass / kAEGetURL ('GURL') Apple event, both at launch and while the app is running.
  • apps/figcraft/src/args.rs handles figcraft://join?… only as a command-line argument ("what the system passes when a figcraft:// link is opened"). That is true on Linux and Windows, but not on macOS.
  • apps/figcraft/src/apple_events.rs (#289) registers handlers through fmv-macos-events 0.1.0. poll matches only Event::Open(paths) and Event::Quit, so a GURL event is never received or routed to the join flow.
  • Info.plist does register the scheme (CFBundleURLTypes → figcraft), so macOS sends the link to FigCraft, and the app then drops it.

Suggested fix

Handle the GURL Apple event (in fmv-macos-events, or next to the existing odoc handler). Pass its URL to the same code path that args.rs uses for a figcraft://join?… argument, then join as Join live session does. The handler has to be registered before the event loop starts, like the odoc one, so that a cold launch from a link is caught too.

Environment

  • FigCraft 0.8.0 (FigCraftBuildCommit 594dc8c), installed in /Applications
  • macOS 27.0
  • lsregister -dump shows /Applications/FigCraft.app as the only handler for figcraft:
  • Server: self-hosted figcraft-server on the LAN; links come from its edit-link share

#923 Binding a colour variable to a solid paint drops the paint's opacity (regression from #804)

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-20 by frodeanonsen · updated 2026-10-20

Summary

Since #804 (fix for #802), binding a colour variable to a solid fill or stroke resets the paint's opacity to 1. An opacity the paint had before the bind is lost. A script that builds a translucent tint, a solid paint at opacity 0.15 bound to a status colour token, now draws the token at full strength.

rebind_paint_alpha(..., bind: true) in crates/engine/src/cmd/styles.rs sets p.opacity = 1.0 unconditionally. Its doc comment says an opacity set while bound stays, but an opacity set before the bind is treated as alpha split out of a typed colour and dropped. The two cases cannot be told apart, because Paint::solid stores the colour opaque with its alpha in opacity.

Environment

  • figcraft-cli built from main at dd6bd3fe, Linux x86_64
  • Not reproducible with the v0.6.0 or v0.7.0 release tarballs (figcraft-0.7.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz): v0.7.0 was tagged before 018b8166 (#804) landed

Steps to reproduce

steps.json:

[
 {"command":"variable.createCollection","params":{"name":"Tokens","modes":["Light"]}},
 {"command":"variable.create","params":{"collection":"Tokens","name":"red","type":"color","value":"#FF0000"}},
 {"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"rectangle","x":0,"y":0,"width":40,"height":40,"props":{"fills":[{"type":"solid","color":"#000000","opacity":0.15}]}}},
 {"command":"node.get","params":{"id":2}},
 {"command":"variable.bind","params":{"ids":[2],"field":"fill","variable":"red"}},
 {"command":"node.get","params":{"id":2}}
]
figcraft-cli run steps.json --no-system-fonts

Expected

The bind replaces the colour and keeps the paint opacity, as in v0.7.0:

"fills":[{"color":"#000000","opacity":0.15000000596046448,"type":"solid"}]
"fills":[{"color":"#FF0000","opacity":0.15000000596046448,"type":"solid"}]

Actual

On main the opacity is gone after the bind:

"fills":[{"color":"#000000","opacity":0.15000000596046448,"type":"solid"}]
"fills":[{"color":"#FF0000","type":"solid"}]

Exported, the 15 % tint renders as a solid fill in the token colour. In our component library, badges whose label uses the same token as the tinted background become solid blocks with an invisible label.

Notes

  • Setting the opacity after variable.bind keeps it, so scripts can work around this by reordering. A paint opacity chosen before binding is still a plausible thing to want to keep, for example a tint whose colour comes from a variable.
  • One way to keep #802 fixed without losing this: reset the opacity on bind only when the paint holds a typed colour's alpha. That needs the paint to record whether its opacity came from Paint::solid or was set explicitly; the opacity value alone can't tell.

#778 Windows: UI blurs in restored window with DX12 backend

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-17 by YarilaFox · updated 2026-10-17

Problem

On Windows, FigCraft's UI text and icons become visibly softer when the app is in a restored (non-maximized) window. Maximizing the same window makes them sharp again. This is reproducible in FigCraft 0.6.0 on a 2560×1440 display at Windows scale 100%.

Reproduction

  1. Open FigCraft on Windows with the default graphics backend.
  2. Compare sidebar text and icons in a maximized window and a restored window.
  3. The restored window looks blurred even after several seconds without resizing or moving it.

Backend isolation

  • Forcing WGPU_BACKEND=dx12 reproduces the soft windowed output.
  • Forcing WGPU_BACKEND=gl keeps the windowed output sharp on the same machine and app build.
  • Capturing FigCraft's internal rendered framebuffer shows sharp text in both window states. The difference appears when that framebuffer is presented on screen with the DX12 backend.
  • A controlled crop of the internal screenshot and Windows PrintWindow capture matched exactly with GL after integer alignment. With DX12 in restored mode, the same crop did not match (about 82.8% exact pixels).

This isolates the symptom to the DX12 presentation/composition path on this setup. It does not yet prove that Direct3D itself or a specific DXGI swap-chain setting is the root cause.

Scope checked

  • Confirmed: 2560×1440 display at 100% Windows scale, restored versus maximized window.
  • Not yet checked: a separate 1920×1080 display or Windows scaling at 125–200%.

Related to #540 in that both concern readability on 1440p, but this report is specifically about a sharpness change when the window is restored.

fixed in

storytold/photocraft#7177 and #779

3 comments
ticket-craft[bot] · 2026-10-17

Possibly related: storytold/filmcraft#1305 and storytold/photocraft#1788.

YarilaFox · 2026-10-17

Follow-up: I isolated a DX12-side fix on the same 2560×1440, 100% scale Windows machine.

wgpu-hal 30.0.1 currently creates the DX12 swap chain with DXGI_SCALING_STRETCH (src/dx12/mod.rs, in Surface::configure). I rebuilt the same FigCraft source and forced WGPU_BACKEND=dx12, changing only this value to DXGI_SCALING_NONE in a local experimental copy of wgpu-hal.

Results: in restored windows sized 1440×900 and 1000×750, the internal UI screenshot and Windows PrintWindow capture were pixel-identical after integer alignment (MAE 0). The original DX12 build showed resampling in the restored window. Restoring the window after maximizing also remained pixel-identical. A normal desktop screenshot showed the maximized UI; the earlier black PrintWindow capture in maximized mode was a limitation of that capture method, not an app display failure.

Microsoft documents DXGI_SCALING_NONE as displaying the back buffer without scaling when target sizes differ: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/dxgi1_2/ne-dxgi1_2-dxgi_scaling

This confirms the swap-chain scaling mode as the cause on this setup. The experiment only covers this Windows/GPU/DPI combination. I am checking a maintainable way to carry the change, since the setting lives in wgpu-hal, not FigCraft's own source.

#754 There's no way to get a missing free font from inside FigCraft

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-17 by Nael-Nathanael · updated 2026-10-17

Summary

When a design uses a free font that isn't on your computer, FigCraft can't get it for you. You have to find the font online, download and install it yourself, then restart FigCraft. Until then the text looks wrong. FigCraft should offer to download free fonts like these. It should only go online when you ask it to.

Evidence

The same test file in FigCraft (left) and in OpenPencil (right). The boxed lines use Pinyon Script and Instrument Serif, two free Google Fonts that aren't installed here. FigCraft draws them in Inter. OpenPencil fetched both fonts by itself and draws them as designed.

Details

Split from #752, as ticket-craft asked there. #752 covers telling the user which fonts are missing; this issue covers getting them. Figma serves Google Fonts from the cloud. OpenPencil 0.16.0 fetches missing families from Google Fonts and Fontsource automatically.

Proposal. The README promises that FigCraft "contacts no server until you share or join a file", so the download only happens when the user asks:

  • A Download button in the Missing fonts window from #752, and a text.downloadFonts {families, confirm: true} command for the MCP server and the control channel. Without confirm: true it sends nothing.
  • Source: the google/fonts repository on GitHub. Each family has a METADATA.pb listing its licence (OFL, Apache 2.0 or UFL) and its whole font files. The CSS API needs every style named up front and gives no licence, and Fontsource splits each family into per-subset files.
  • Each file is checked before it is kept: it must parse as a font and name the requested family.
  • Files are saved with their licence in the per-user font folder FigCraft already scans (~/.local/share/fonts, ~/Library/Fonts, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Fonts), under FigCraft/<Family>/. The next launch and figcraft-cli find them without any new code. On Linux and macOS other apps see them too; on Windows they don't, because a font there also needs a registry entry, which FigCraft doesn't write. The MCP server has no fonts folder, so fonts it downloads last for its session.
  • The window says what is sent: the family names, to GitHub.
  • A build can leave the feature out with an empty FIGCRAFT_FONT_LIBRARY, as FIGCRAFT_DEFAULT_SERVER does for the share server.
  • The browser build is not covered: it would need a fetch-based transport.

If maintainers would rather keep downloaded fonts in FigCraft's own folder, or use another source, that's an easy change before merge.

A fix is in #764, stacked on #758.

#702 Command/Ctrl-resizing an image layer recentres the fill instead of cropping

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-16 by timrrrr · updated 2026-10-16

Reproduction

On macOS (FigCraft 0.6.0, also reproduced in the engine on current main at d1d8c3f652cea20bee02bdbc3ded9a2f5362ba08):

  1. Place a rectangular image with a clearly identifiable left and right side.
  2. Select its image-filled layer with the Move tool.
  3. Hold Command and drag the right edge inward to half the layer's width. The corresponding modifier on other platforms is Ctrl.

Expected

Only the visible area narrows: the left side of the image keeps its position and scale, and the right side is hidden. The original image bytes remain available for later crop adjustments. An ordinary resize without the modifier keeps its existing behaviour.

Actual

The layer becomes narrower, but its Fill placement is recalculated for the new bounds. The image recentres instead of staying in place. For a synthetic 200 × 100 image cropped to 100 × 100, the first displayed source column changes from 0 to 50.

Evidence and scope

A pointer-gesture regression on main reproduces the pixel mismatch. A second regression shows that the fill stays in Fill mode rather than receiving a crop transform. Existing transform tests and the ordinary resize / Scale tool controls pass.

This report concerns cropping an image fill by resizing the layer's bounds; the existing Command/Ctrl behaviour for ignoring a frame's child constraints is a separate operation.

The quick-crop modifier is described in the public crop documentation. No implementation code or private application data from another product was inspected.

Desktop reproduction

The same synthetic image in a separate build of the baseline, before and after a Command-drag of the right edge from 600 to 300. The left edge stays at x = 0, but the image recentres.

Before the gesture Baseline after the gesture

Proposed fix scope

The initial fix targets a single non-text layer outside auto layout, with Fill/Fit/Crop image fills. Text, auto-layout contexts, Tile fills, multiple selected layers and the Scale tool retain their existing behaviour. Text reflow and auto layout can recompute the layer bounds after a resize, so those cases need separate work. This is not a claim of complete interaction parity.

Implementation: PR #703, with the bounded scope above, regression tests and a desktop demonstration.

#688 Plugin permission to save a file through a host-owned dialog (enables exporters, e.g. After Effects)

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-16 by seedik13 · updated 2026-10-16

Hi! I'm a FigCraft user and I'd like to help grow the plugin ecosystem.

Problem
Plugins are sandboxed with no file access, and dialogs are off limits
(docs/target-app-parity.md). That's the right security default, but it
means a plugin can't produce any output file, so exporters are impossible
(After Effects, Lottie, code, sprite sheets, JSON for other tools...).

Proposal
A new optional manifest permission (name is just a suggestion: saveFile).

  • The plugin hands the host a file name suggestion, a MIME type and the bytes.
  • The host opens its own Save dialog; the user picks where it goes.
  • The plugin never gets a path and never touches the disk, so the
    sandbox guarantee stays the same.
  • The permission is shown in the install confirmation, like the others.
  • Works on the web build too (browser download instead of a dialog).

Motivating example: "Export to After Effects"
A plugin with read access to the selected frames walks the node tree
(frames, groups, shapes, text, positions, fills) and generates an
After Effects ExtendScript (.jsx) that rebuilds each frame as a composition
with shape layers, text layers and parented nulls for groups.
The user selects frames, runs Plugins > Export to After Effects, picks where
to save the .jsx, then runs it in After Effects (File > Scripts > Run Script File).
Without saveFile this plugin can't exist; with it, it's a single WASM
module that works on every platform.

Questions

  1. Is this direction OK for you, or would you prefer something else
    (e.g. a clipboard permission, or a host-side "export" extension point)?
  2. Where should it live (manifest schema, plugin ABI, the plugin.* commands)?
  3. Would you accept a PR with the permission plus an example plugin
    (like the existing Tidy names / Swatch grid ones)?

Happy to do the work if you're on board. Thanks!

#658 Canvas keeps the page colour of the theme it was made in, not the current theme

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-16 by ahmedhosnypro · updated 2026-10-16

Summary

With the interface theme on System (or switched manually), the panels follow the theme but the middle pane — the canvas — does not: a file made (or first opened) while the app was dark keeps its dark canvas in a light interface, and a file made light stays light in dark mode. Only new files took the current theme's page colour; an existing page's colour never changed, and a file opened before the theme was known kept whatever colour was stored.

Cause

The canvas colour is the page background (crates/render/src/lib.rs), a per-page document property. By design it was frozen when the file/page was made (Session::set_ui_dark only recoloured an untouched blank file once, on the first report of a dark theme); theme_pages_tests pinned this as "a change of theme never repaints a page".

That diverges from the incumbent: in Figma a page still on its default background follows the live UI theme (that is why dark mode darkens the canvas at all), while a page whose background was explicitly chosen keeps its colour.

Proposed fix

Treat the two theme-given colours (Color::DEFAULT_PAGE #F5F5F5, Color::DARK_PAGE #1E1E1E) as "default":

  • When the effective theme changes, repaint every page still on the opposite default to the current theme's default, in every open document — including files opened before the theme was known.
  • Chosen page colours (page.setBackground) are left alone; headless sessions (CLI, MCP, exports) keep the light default.
  • The repaint is no edit: no undo step, nothing marked dirty to save (the last-saved snapshot is repainted with it; the file on disk keeps its colour until the next save, and reopening in the other theme repaints again).

Known edge: a page explicitly coloured exactly the other theme's default is indistinguishable from a default page in the file format and follows the theme too.

#648 [Feature Request] Auto layout: per-child margin and align-self

maintainer labelmultiple issues · opened 2026-10-16 by Anirte · updated 2026-10-16

Summary

FigCraft's auto layout covers most of flexbox, but two per-child properties that websites use constantly are missing: margin and align-self. Right now both have to be faked with wrapper frames or spacer layers, which changes the layer structure and makes the design harder to map to real CSS.

Adding them would bring the layout model closer to what ends up in the browser.

Requested

1. margin on auto layout children

  • marginTop, marginRight, marginBottom, marginLeft (plus marginHorizontal / marginVertical shorthands).
  • Taken into account by the parent's layout like CSS margins (hug/fill sizing, wrapping, grid cells).
  • Usable with variables (like gap and padding).

2. alignSelf on auto layout children

  • Values: auto | start | center | end | stretch (mapping to the existing min | center | max plus fill on the cross axis).
  • Overrides the parent's crossAlign for that one child.

Why

  • Typical UI pieces need "this one element is aligned differently" (an icon at the end of a row, a badge at the top, a label centered in a column of left-aligned items).
  • A single extra gap below one item (margin-bottom) is very common in components.
  • Today the workaround is an extra wrapper frame with padding or a fixed-size spacer. That adds layers that don't exist in the real UI and breaks the 1:1 mapping to CSS.
  • It would improve inspect.code output (CSS / HTML / React) and make design-to-code and import from other tools more faithful.

Current workarounds

  • Margin: wrapper frame with padding, or a spacer layer between siblings.
  • align-self: wrapper frame with fill sizing and its own alignment, or absolute positioning.

#622 System theme mode always draws light on Linux and the BSDs

maintainer labelshared · opened 2026-10-16 by ahmedhosnypro · updated 2026-10-23

Summary

With Preferences theme set to System (the default), the interface ignores the desktop's dark mode on Linux and the BSDs and always draws light. Windows, macOS and the web app follow the system correctly.

Cause

The UI resolves the system preference from Context::system_theme() (crates/ui-egui/src/lib.rs). That value comes from eframe/winit, and winit 0.30 never reports a system theme on Linux or the BSDs: EventLoop::system_theme() is hardcoded None, X11's window.theme() likewise, and no ThemeChanged event is ever delivered there. So the comparison is always false and the light fallback wins. This is a known upstream gap (rust-windowing/winit#4403).

Proposed fix

When the windowing stack reports no theme, fall back to the freedesktop colour scheme:

  • Read org.freedesktop.portal.Settings / org.freedesktop.appearance / color-scheme (1 = dark, 2 = light) from the settings portal — implemented by both GNOME and KDE Plasma 6 on X11 and Wayland.
  • Watch the portal's SettingChanged signal so a live appearance switch follows without restarting.
  • The OS theme keeps winning where winit does report one (macOS, Windows, web); without any answer the existing light fallback stands.

Environment

  • Linux, KDE Plasma 6 (also reproducible on any Linux/BSD desktop)
  • eframe 0.36 / winit 0.30

#609 [Feature Request] Real-Time Collaborative Editing for FigCraft and the ArtCraft Suite

maintainer labelsharedmultiple issues · opened 2026-10-15 by wjywbs · updated 2026-10-15

Summary

I would like to request a complete, production-ready collaborative editing experience for FigCraft, powered by a common, open-source collaboration server shared across the entire ArtCraft suite.

The goal is to allow designers, developers, product managers, and other collaborators to work together on the same design files in real time. Users should be able to see each other's cursors and selections, edit designs simultaneously, invite teammates, discuss changes through contextual comments, share component libraries, explore alternative designs, review interactive prototypes, and hand completed designs off to development.

This should build on FigCraft's existing collaboration work and evolve it into a reliable platform that can also serve FilmCraft, PhotoCraft, VectorCraft, LightCraft, PdfCraft, EffectCraft, DesignCraft, and future ArtCraft applications.

Rather than implementing separate collaboration infrastructure for every application, I propose a shared, open-source server, protocol, and reusable client library that all ArtCraft applications can use.

The server should be self-hostable on a local network, a remote server, or public or private cloud infrastructure. Users should not need a proprietary cloud service, mandatory online account, or subscription to collaborate.

The vision is to make real-time collaboration a fundamental capability of the ArtCraft ecosystem while preserving its open-source, local-first philosophy and giving users full control over their infrastructure and data.

This request complements the broader suite-wide proposal in [FilmCraft #350](storytold/filmcraft#350).

1. Real-Time Multiplayer Design

Multiple users should be able to open and edit the same FigCraft document simultaneously, with changes appearing in real time.

For example, one designer could create page layouts while another develops reusable components, adjusts typography, configures variables, or refines illustrations. Everyone should see updates immediately without manually exchanging files or repeatedly refreshing the document.

Requested capabilities include:

  • Live cursors, user names, avatars, selections, and visible editing activity.
  • Following another collaborator's viewport during demonstrations or design reviews.
  • Spotlight or presentation functionality to direct collaborators' attention to a specific area.
  • Clear indications when another user is editing the same object or text.
  • Real-time synchronization of frames, layers, vector objects, components, variants, styles, variables, and prototype connections.
  • Per-user undo and redo that preserve other collaborators' independent work.
  • Reliable reconnection and recovery after network interruptions.
  • Consistent document state across connected clients.

The objective is to make simultaneous editing feel natural, allowing multiple people to contribute to one design without constantly coordinating who can edit or exchanging duplicate project files.

2. Sharing, Invitations, and Permissions

Sharing a design should be as straightforward as inviting teammates through a link.

A typical workflow would be:

  1. The document owner selects Share.
  2. They choose the appropriate access level, such as editor or viewer.
  3. They share an invitation link or code with their teammates.
  4. Collaborators join the session using the configured authentication and access rules.
  5. The owner can update permissions or revoke access when needed.

The system should support team members and, where permitted, guest reviewers who do not need full editing privileges.

A viewer should be able to inspect the design, navigate pages, explore permitted prototypes, and participate in reviews without modifying the underlying document.

Over time, persistent identities, teams, workspaces, and project-level permissions should make it possible to manage access across many projects rather than treating every document as an isolated collaboration session.

Sharing should work both on a local network and remotely, using the same collaboration infrastructure.

3. Contextual Comments and Design Reviews

Feedback should happen directly within the design environment instead of being scattered across emails, messages, screenshots, and external task trackers.

For example, a product manager could pin a comment to a button, request a different label, mention the responsible designer, and follow the discussion until the change is completed.

Requested capabilities include:

  • Comments attached to frames, layers, objects, or specific design locations.
  • Threaded replies, mentions, reactions, and comment resolution.
  • Notifications for relevant comments and outstanding feedback.
  • Direct links to specific documents, pages, frames, or review locations.
  • Clear visibility into unresolved feedback.
  • Review workflows that do not require granting full editing permissions.
  • Persistent comments and review history synchronized across collaborators.

These features would allow stakeholders to participate in the design process without interrupting the people actively editing the document.

4. Shared Components, Styles, Variables, and Libraries

Collaborative design requires a consistent design system that can be reused across projects and maintained by a team.

FigCraft should support shared libraries containing reusable components, component variants, styles, typography, colors, and design variables.

For example, a design-system maintainer could update a shared button component while application designers use that component in multiple files. Designers should be able to discover the update, inspect the changes, and update their instances without manually recreating the component in every project.

Requested capabilities include:

  • Shared component and asset libraries.
  • Publishing, updating, and consuming library assets.
  • Reusable styles, variables, and component properties.
  • Visibility into library versions and changes.
  • Updating component instances when source definitions change.
  • Identification of outdated, missing, or overridden library assets.
  • Preservation of appropriate instance customizations during updates.
  • Team-wide library discovery and permission management.

Library changes should be traceable, with sufficient information for designers to understand what has changed before accepting updates.

5. Branching, Version History, and Collaborative Review

Designers should be able to explore alternatives without putting the primary design at risk.

For example, one designer could experiment with a new onboarding flow while another continues working on the main design. Once the alternative is reviewed, the team could selectively merge the accepted changes.

Useful capabilities include:

  • Creating a branch from a known version of a design.
  • Making independent changes without immediately affecting the main document.
  • Comparing revisions and inspecting changes between branches.
  • Reviewing conflicting edits when multiple people modify the same content.
  • Merging accepted changes into the primary design.
  • Maintaining revision history and named checkpoints.
  • Restoring earlier versions when necessary.
  • Attributing changes to individual collaborators.

FigCraft's existing work on branching, review, merging, and version history could provide a foundation for extending these workflows to collaborative sessions.

The implementation should prioritize document integrity and predictable merging rather than silently overwriting conflicting work.

6. Interactive Prototypes and Stakeholder Presentations

Designers should be able to share interactive prototypes with teammates and stakeholders without giving everyone permission to edit the source document.

For example, a designer could share a mobile application flow with a product manager, who can navigate between screens, test interactions, and leave comments about specific steps.

Requested capabilities include:

  • Sharing a prototype or a particular starting flow.
  • Presentation and read-only viewing modes.
  • Testing navigation, transitions, overlays, and interactive components.
  • Direct links to relevant flows or presentation contexts where practical.
  • Comments associated with relevant frames or design elements.
  • Reliable updates to the shared prototype as the source design changes.
  • A clear distinction between reviewing a prototype and editing its source document.

This would make stakeholder reviews more interactive and reduce the need to export screenshots or create separate copies of a design for feedback.

7. Developer Handoff and Design Inspection

Collaboration should continue after a design is approved, allowing developers to inspect and implement it accurately.

A designer could mark a component or frame as ready for development. Developers could then inspect dimensions, spacing, typography, colors, variables, component properties, and exportable assets, with a clear indication of the version being handed off.

Useful capabilities include:

  • Read-only design inspection.
  • Ready-for-development status and annotations.
  • Access to relevant design tokens, variables, styles, and component properties.
  • Exportable assets and reusable component references.
  • Visibility into recent changes and unresolved review comments.
  • Stable links to specific frames and components.
  • Clear communication between design and development teams.

This would help prevent implementation errors caused by outdated screenshots, copied specifications, or uncertainty about which revision is approved.

8. A Common Open-Source Collaboration Server

Instead of implementing separate collaboration backends for every application, I propose developing a common collaboration server that can power the entire ArtCraft suite.

The server should be:

  • Fully open source under a license compatible with the ArtCraft ecosystem.
  • Self-hostable without mandatory subscriptions, accounts, or external services.
  • Available as a native binary and through Docker or Podman, with documented container deployment.
  • Usable on a local network without internet connectivity.
  • Accessible remotely through secure connections.
  • Deployable on a workstation, NAS, home server, VPS, private data center, or public or private cloud.
  • Capable of supporting multiple applications, users, projects, and sessions concurrently.
  • Suitable for private and air-gapped environments where practical.

A small team should be able to run the server on a local machine or NAS. A distributed team should be able to deploy the same software on a remote server. Both should use the same protocol and core functionality.

The core collaboration capabilities should remain available to self-hosters without requiring a Storytold-operated service.

9. A Shared Protocol and Reusable Client Library

The server should provide common collaboration infrastructure while each application retains its own document model, file format, and editing semantics.

A reusable Rust client library and shared protocol could handle:

  • Connections, sessions, and presence.
  • Project discovery, sharing, and permissions.
  • Real-time change propagation.
  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Reconnection and state recovery.
  • Revision metadata and persistence interfaces.
  • Common collaboration events and notifications.
  • Shared identity, workspace, and asset references.

Each application should provide its own synchronization adapter. FigCraft's design objects, component hierarchies, and variable systems have different requirements from FilmCraft's timelines or PhotoCraft's layers and adjustments.

Possible synchronization approaches include CRDTs, operational transformation, semantic operation logs, or hybrid strategies. The best approach may differ between applications and document operations.

The architectural principle should be one common collaboration platform, with application-specific synchronization logic, rather than forcing every application to use an identical internal document representation.

The work should coordinate with the suite-wide effort described in FilmCraft Issue 350 and any common infrastructure already under development. The goal is to converge on one server and protocol rather than develop competing implementations.

10. Local-First Editing and Flexible Storage

Collaboration should enhance FigCraft's local-first workflow, not replace it.

Users should still be able to create, edit, save, and export local .figcraft files without signing in or running a collaboration server.

When collaboration is enabled, the system should support:

  • Local-network collaboration without an internet connection.
  • Server-managed project storage and persistent shared documents.
  • Shared filesystem or NAS workflows where appropriate.
  • Optional S3-compatible object storage and asset synchronization.
  • Reliable recovery after network interruptions.
  • Safe handling of independent offline edits.
  • Local backups and explicit export or detachment from a server.

Large assets should not need to be transferred again whenever only a small document change occurs. Applications should be able to synchronize document operations independently of large referenced assets where appropriate.

Concurrent and offline changes should be reconciled safely, with conflicts surfaced for review whenever automatic merging is inappropriate.

11. Shared Workspaces and Cross-Application Collaboration

Over time, the collaboration server should provide common workspace services across the ArtCraft suite.

Potential capabilities include:

  • User accounts, teams, and workspaces.
  • Project invitations and membership.
  • Owner, administrator, editor, reviewer, and viewer roles.
  • Revocable sharing and guest access.
  • Persistent version history, checkpoints, and restoration.
  • Attribution showing who changed what and when.
  • Backup, recovery, and export tools.
  • Optional integration with established identity providers.
  • Shared project metadata and asset references.

This would also enable workflows across different ArtCraft applications. For example, designers could use VectorCraft illustrations in FigCraft documents while keeping track of source assets, or coordinate related design and video projects through a common workspace.

The applications do not need to share a document format. Instead, the infrastructure can provide shared identities, permissions, metadata, asset references, and collaboration services while each application remains responsible for its own content.

12. Security and Privacy

Self-hosting is particularly important for individuals, design studios, and organizations working with confidential projects.

The collaboration infrastructure should provide:

  • Encrypted connections for remote access.
  • Appropriate authentication and authorization.
  • Secure sharing with revocable access.
  • Configurable network restrictions.
  • Reliable backup and recovery.
  • Clear ownership and export of project data.
  • No mandatory telemetry or third-party cloud dependency.
  • Support for private and air-gapped deployments where practical.

Users should know where their files are stored, who can access them, and which services receive their data.

A hosted ArtCraft service could be offered as an optional convenience in the future, but the core collaboration infrastructure and self-hosting option should remain available to the community.

13. Suggested Implementation Plan

This is a substantial undertaking, so it does not need to be implemented all at once.

A reasonable progression could be:

  1. Establish the shared architecture: Define the common protocol, client library, server responsibilities, and application adapter contracts in coordination with the work described in FilmCraft Issue 350.
  2. Harden FigCraft collaboration: Improve the existing implementation with reliable synchronization, reconnect behavior, conflict handling, persistence, and access controls.
  3. Deliver essential collaborative design workflows: Focus on simultaneous editing, share links, permissions, presence, comments, presentation, and reliable undo and redo.
  4. Add team design workflows: Extend collaboration to shared libraries, version history, branching, merging, and developer handoff.
  5. Standardize self-hosted deployment: Provide documentation and straightforward deployment options for local networks, remote servers, and cloud infrastructure.
  6. Integrate other ArtCraft applications: Reuse the same server and core client library with application-specific synchronization and testing.
  7. Expand shared workspace capabilities: Introduce unified project management, team administration, identity integration, and cross-application asset references.

The maintainers can decide the precise scope and order of these milestones. The important thing is to design for the entire suite from the beginning while delivering useful improvements to FigCraft early.

Expected Outcome

The goal is to make FigCraft a fully collaborative design environment where teams can edit the same document in real time, share reusable design systems, exchange contextual feedback, explore alternative designs, review interactive prototypes, and hand approved work off to development.

All of this should be powered by a common, open-source collaboration platform that users can host on their own local network, remote server, or preferred cloud infrastructure.

The same infrastructure should eventually power collaboration throughout ArtCraft, allowing improvements to benefit every application rather than duplicating development effort in each project.

I would love to see real-time collaboration become a foundational capability of FigCraft and the entire ArtCraft ecosystem, with a shared, self-hostable server that keeps users in control of their own creative workflows and data.

Thank you for considering this request and for building an open-source creative suite.

#571 Turn on the MCP / control channel from the app (no --control needed)

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-15 by diegoaces · updated 2026-10-15

Problem

Driving the desktop app from an AI agent (figcraft-cli mcp --attach <port>) needs the app to be started from a terminal with figcraft --control <port> (or FIGCRAFT_CONTROL_PORT). People who open FigCraft from the Dock, Finder or the Start menu have no way to turn the channel on, and nothing in the app tells them how to configure their MCP client.

Proposal

A Help ▸ Connect an AI agent (MCP)… window (also in the canvas ? menu) that:

  • shows whether the channel is on (listening on 127.0.0.1:7979) and turns it on with one click (port 7979, or the saved mcp_port);
  • has a Turn on when FigCraft opens checkbox, kept in the preferences (mcp_on_launch, off by default);
  • shows the MCP client settings (Claude Desktop claude_desktop_config.json, .mcp.json) with the real path of figcraft-cli (next to the app, else on PATH) and a Copy button;
  • says why when the port is taken.

--control keeps working as today. The channel still listens on 127.0.0.1 only, and one channel per app (once on, it stays on that port).

Commands

  • help.mcp: opens the window (UI request, dropped on the control channel like other dialogs)
  • app.mcpStart {port?}: asks the app to start the channel; a no-op headless
  • pref.mcpOnLaunch {on?}

Notes

  • Desktop only: new Services methods (control_port, control_start, mcp_cli_path) default to "not available", so the web build is unaffected.
  • On macOS figcraft-cli ships in its own zip, not inside FigCraft.app, hence the PATH lookup.
  • Milestone: M0.9 (MCP).

I have an implementation ready (engine, UI, control server, en/es strings, tests, docs) and can open a PR if this direction sounds right.

Hamza0101 · 2026-10-20

Picked up the piece you kept this issue open for — per-kind counts — in #951. @MarekSpodBiedry's worry about new plumbing turned out not to apply: the convention already exists on the other side of the same crate.

The REST importer counts repeats (Warnings in crates/format/src/rest/mod.rs: distinct notes in first-seen order, (×n) appended in finish()), and ui-egui's note_text already reads that suffix off before it looks the base up in the catalogue. The .fig mapper had its own dedupe with no counting — !self.warnings.contains(&w) — so its notes named each kind once and said nothing about how much of the file they covered. That is exactly what you saw: one line, while 83 text layers lost leadingTrim.

The mapper now uses the same collector. No note text changes (so every catalogue key stays a key), the cap and first-seen order are the same, and a note is still a string — so figcraft-cli info, the import report and file.open's warnings all gain the counts without a shape change.

Measured, with the count dropped again to check the test bites:

["connector layers import as static frame/vector snapshots with labels when present; …",
 "connector label was skipped: depth limit prevents nested snapshot children"]

Two notes, plain, where the fix reports the repeated one as … (×2).

One thing I did not do, since it is a maintainer call and you framed it as one: I did not add a separate taxonomy of "dropped" versus "approximated". Every note the importers already emit gets a count; nothing is reclassified. If you want info to group them under headings as well, that is a further step and I am happy to take it.

The .fig export warnings (fig/export.rs) still dedupe without counting; the i18n test excludes that file and this issue is about import, so I left them.

  • Presenting the prototype places the overlay there.

#298 Fonts activated through Adobe Fonts are not indexed; text silently falls back

classified in this triage · opened 2026-10-14 by nes-cape · updated 2026-10-16

Triage note: Fonts activated by a font manager (Adobe Fonts) aren't indexed on macOS; text silently falls back. VectorCraft fixed the same thing in its #579 (enumerate CoreText's available fonts, not just font folders); port that approach (clean-room, no shared code) and warn when a font falls back.

What happens

Text in a font activated through Adobe Fonts (for example Neue Haas Grotesk Text Pro) renders in the fallback font, without a warning. The render is byte-identical to one with a font name that does not exist. macOS lists the family as available (CTFontManagerCopyAvailableFontFamilyNames). A copy of the same font file in ~/Library/Fonts renders correctly.

Expected

Fonts that macOS reports as available, including ones activated by a font manager, are indexed. VectorCraft finds them since #579.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Activate a family in Adobe Fonts (Creative Cloud), e.g. Neue Haas Grotesk Text Pro.
  2. Script a.json: [{"command":"frame.create","params":{"x":0,"y":0,"width":800,"height":200,"name":"F"}},{"command":"text.create","params":{"text":"Hamburgefonstiv","x":20,"y":40,"parent":2,"props":{"fontFamily":"Neue Haas Grotesk Text Pro","fontSize":64}}}]
  3. figcraft-cli run a.json --out a.figcraft && figcraft-cli render a.figcraft -o a.png
  4. Repeat with "fontFamily":"No Such Font" as b: a.png and b.png are identical.

Version

FigCraft 0.5.1, CLI, macOS universal, macOS 26.1 (25B78)

1 comment
AganzeFelicite · 2026-10-16

I've opened a fix for this in #661 (waiting for review).

Cause: Creative Cloud doesn't install activated fonts into a font folder. It keeps them in ~/Library/Application Support/Adobe/CoreSync/plugins/livetype/.r/ as hidden files named by number, often without an extension. FigCraft only scanned the standard font folders and only read .ttf/.otf/.ttc/.otc files, so these fonts were never indexed and text fell back silently.

Fix: on macOS the font scan now includes that folder, and files without an extension are read when they start like a font file. Fonts are read in place while they're active in Creative Cloud; nothing is copied.

I don't have Creative Cloud to test with, so I checked it with a font placed the same way (a hidden, extension-less file in that folder). If you can try the build once it lands, a confirmation with Neue Haas Grotesk Text Pro would be very welcome.

#295 UI and optimization

classified in this triage · opened 2026-10-14 by darabon · updated 2026-10-14

Triage note: Three things: canvas stays grey in dark theme (duplicate of #658), zoom-in/out shows re-render lag especially with glass effects, and off-screen objects appear cut off during zoom (tile/visibility culling). Overlaps #501 (glass, blur, and performance).

If you set the dark theme in the program, the background in editing mode remains gray, as in the white theme.

If you zoom in very close to objects and then zoom out, you'll notice loading lag. This is most noticeable if you use an object with a glass effect. I assume the program calculates the rendering of each object every frame or every camera move to conserve RAM. It's like if an object isn't visible, it doesn't load. But here it turns out that outside the visibility zone, objects not only don't load, but are actually cut off. This kind of optimization is necessary in large and complex projects. I suggest abandoning this kind of wild "optimization" and storing all objects in the loaded scene in RAM. This program doesn't really put enough strain on the computer to perform such optimizations. It forces the processor and video card to recalculate the appearance of each object. Also, if you zoom out very much, you can see gray areas where the project didn't load.

The "community" and "drafts" side tabs don't work in the "home" tab.

#286 Number fields: optional scroll-wheel stepping (FigCraft extension)

classified in this triage · opened 2026-10-14 by mesidex · updated 2026-10-14

Triage note: Well-specified FigCraft extension: optional scroll-wheel stepping on focused number fields, off by default, one undo step per gesture. Low risk, ready to implement as written.

Description:
Not a Figma behaviour (Figma’s number fields don’t change on wheel), so this is a FigCraft extension. It reuses the existing number-field step rules.

  • With a numeric field focused, the wheel or trackpad over it steps the value: up increments, down decrements.
  • Steps and modifiers match scrubbing and arrow keys (nudge preferences as base, Shift x10, Alt x0.1).
  • An unfocused field never captures the wheel, so the Design panel keeps scrolling normally. Canvas zoom/pan are unchanged.
  • Respects min/max, units and rounding. On Mixed values, each layer steps relative to its own value.
  • Trackpads accumulate fractional deltas into whole steps and follow the OS scroll direction.
  • One scroll gesture is one undo step (idle timeout, pointer leave or modifier change ends it).
  • Preferences toggle to enable it. Default to be decided (suggest off).

Open questions:

  • Should a scroll edit detach a variable binding, as typing does?
  • Focus-only, or hover plus a modifier?

#1138 [Feature Request] Please add official OpenCode skill support for FigCraft

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-22 by AHL8192 · updated 2026-10-22

Feature request: ship an official OpenCode skill

This is a feature request, not a support question. FigCraft is installed and working here — I don't need help with my setup, my install, or my design file. I'm asking for one directory of markdown to live in the repo.

FigCraft already exposes everything an agent needs: figcraft-cli mcp (18 tools), 569 commands in 57 namespaces, components with variants, styles, variables and Dev Mode. The missing piece is the how to drive it layer — a skill.

MCP server alone MCP server + skill
Auto layout vs. x/y confusion When to set gap/padding/mainAlign instead
opacity: 2 quietly read as 200% Silent reinterpretations, called out
.png path writes a .figcraft file save_file / export rules that catch it
Attached mode + covered window → 60 s timeouts The trap, and the recovery sequence

An MCP server answers "what can this app do?". A skill answers "what should an agent do next, in what order, with which ids, and which footguns should it avoid?" — the same thing your own docs do for a human.

The ask

  • Add .opencode/skills/figcraft/ (SKILL.md + references/ + scripts/) to the repo, versioned with the app
  • One line in the README next to the MCP section with the install command
  • Regenerate the version / tool-count / command-id numbers at release — scripts/probe.sh and scripts/dump-commands.sh do most of it
  • Optional: a --print-skill flag, so installation is one command

The skill — already written and tested against FigCraft 0.8.0

git clone https://github.com/AHL8192/opencode-craft-skills.git
cp -r opencode-craft-skills/figcraft ~/.config/opencode/skills/figcraft
  • Repo: https://github.com/AHL8192/opencode-craft-skills/tree/main/figcraft
  • Unlisted gist mirror: https://gist.github.com/AHL8192/1f8e1760ab17c7b913bcb28e5a07b5df

What it covers, specifically:

  • auto layout: which properties place children, and how to verify with absoluteBounds
  • silent reinterpretation — opacity as percentage, save_file not validating extensions, export writing the requested format
  • the Wayland attached-mode timeout and the recovery that actually works
  • building a component, adding variants, instancing without losing overrides

The references/ folder carries the full command catalogue, connection modes with ports and auth, verified recipes, and a bugs-and-workarounds.md with reproductions. There is also a deliberate "What was not tested" section, because pretending otherwise would be worse than useless.

SKILL.md — full text, click to expand (12 KB) 
---
name: FigCraft
description: Use whenever working with FigCraft on this machine — the Rust interface-design and prototyping app (a Figma-class tool) — including creating or editing frames, auto layout, components and variants, styles and variables, vector networks, prototypes, Dev Mode, importing or exporting (.figcraft, .json, .fig, SVG, PNG/JPG/WebP/PDF), driving the running desktop window, or using its MCP server, `figcraft-cli`, control channel or command engine. Triggers on "FigCraft", "figcraft-cli", "figcraft mcp", "design a screen/landing page/dashboard in FigCraft", "build a component or variant", "wire a prototype flow", "export this design as PNG/SVG/PDF/fig", "take a FigCraft screenshot", "drive the FigCraft window", and requests to automate interface design or FigCraft itself. Invoke with @figcraft.
---

# FigCraft — agent operation

FigCraft is a native Rust interface-design tool: pages, frames, auto layout, components
and variants, vector networks, styles and variables, prototypes and Dev Mode. Every menu
item, tool and gesture is a **command with an id**; the UI, `figcraft-cli`, the JSON control
channel and the MCP server all drive the same engine. Files are `.figcraft` archives.

## Machine snapshot (verified 2026-10-22, 0.8.0)

| Thing | Value |
|---|---|
| Desktop app | `/usr/bin/figcraft` — `FigCraft 0.8.0 (594dc8c6cf50…)` |
| CLI | `/usr/bin/figcraft-cli` — `figcraft-cli 0.8.0` |
| Install | Debian package `figcraft 0.8.0-1` (`dpkg -S /usr/bin/figcraft`) |
| App flags | `--control PORT`, `--automation-read-root DIR`, `--automation-write-root DIR`, `--version`; **`--help` is rejected, `-h` opens the GUI** |
| MCP headless | `figcraft-cli mcp` (18 tools, protocol `2025-06-18`) |
| MCP attached | `figcraft --control 47801` + `figcraft-cli mcp --attach 47801` |
| OpenCode servers | `figcraft` (headless), `figcraft-app` (bridge to 47801) |
| Command catalog | **569 commands in 57 namespaces** (`figcraft-cli commands --json`) |
| Starter templates | 8 (`template.list`): mobile-app, landing-page, dashboard, design-system, wireframe-kit, social-posts, slides, icon-set |
| Formats | native `.figcraft` (zip: `document.json` + `thumbnail.png`), `.json` (FigCraft or REST API file JSON), `.fig` best-effort; import SVG + PNG/JPG/WebP/GIF/BMP/TIF; export PNG/JPG/WebP/SVG/PDF/`.fig` |
| No parity command | `figcraft-cli parity` does not exist |

**Alpha software**: re-verify with the scripts below.

## Mental model

- A **document** has **pages**; pages hold layers. Page 1 has id `1`; new layers usually
  start at `2` and ids keep counting up (they survive save/reload).
- **Coordinates are page units** (1 unit = 1 px at 100% zoom), x right, **y down**.
- `create_node` / `set_properties` `x`/`y` are **relative to the parent frame** (the page when
  there is none). **Groups and boolean groups have no coordinate space of their own** — a layer
  in a group is placed in the frame the group sits in. `get_node` reports `x`/`y` the same way
  plus `absoluteBounds` in page coordinates.
- **Auto layout owns its children's positions.** In an auto-layout frame set `layout`, `gap`,
  `padding`, `mainAlign`, `crossAlign`, `sizingH`/`sizingV` (`fixed|hug|fill`) and the min/max
  sizes instead of x/y. Grid: `layout:"grid"` + `gridColumns`, `columnTracks`, `gridColumn`…
- A **command** is `{"command": id, "params": {…}}`. `list_commands` finds ids and parameter
  docs; `run_command` runs one; `batch` runs many as **one undo step**.
- **Everything mutating is one undo step**, and a failing command leaves the document unchanged.
  `batch` is all-or-nothing.
- **Verify by reading back** (`get_node`, `inspect_document`), never by trusting a success reply:
  several silent-success bugs are listed below.

## Two connection modes

| Mode | Start | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| Headless | `figcraft-cli mcp` | No window. Batch creation, rendering, export, CLI scripts, confined file access. |
| Attached | `figcraft --control 47801` then `figcraft-cli mcp --attach 47801` | Drives the real window: `screenshot {window:true}`, `pointer`, `key`, `type_text`, `inspect_ui`. |

Both speak MCP over stdio. In this OpenCode install they are configured as `figcraft` and
`figcraft-app` in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (add them if missing; see
`references/mcp-and-control.md`). A direct stdio JSON-RPC client works without any config.

```sh
# headless
figcraft-cli mcp
# live window on a port you own (check: ss -ltn | grep 47801)
figcraft --control 47801 &
figcraft-cli mcp --attach 47801
```

## Minimal working example (MCP, headless)

```jsonc
// 1. a frame on the page
{"name":"create_node","arguments":{"type":"frame","name":"Card","x":0,"y":0,"width":320,"height":200,
  "props":{"fill":"#FFFFFF","cornerRadius":12}}}
// → {"id": 2, "node": {...}}
// 2. a text layer inside it (x/y relative to the frame)
{"name":"create_node","arguments":{"type":"text","parent":2,"x":24,"y":32,"text":"Hello FigCraft",
  "props":{"fontSize":28,"fill":"#1B1B1B"}}}
// 3. read it back
{"name":"get_node","arguments":{"id":3,"depth":0}}
{"name":"inspect_document","arguments":{}}
// 4. look at it
{"name":"export","arguments":{"ids":[2],"format":"png","scale":2,"path":"/tmp/card.png"}}
// 5. save
{"name":"save_file","arguments":{"path":"/tmp/card.figcraft"}}
```

The same document from the shell, without MCP:

```sh
cat > /tmp/card.json <<'JSON'
[{"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"frame","name":"Card","width":320,"height":200,
   "props":{"fill":"#FFFFFF","cornerRadius":12}}},
 {"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"text","parent":{"$step":0},"x":24,"y":32,
   "text":"Hello FigCraft","props":{"fontSize":28}}}]
JSON
figcraft-cli run /tmp/card.json --out /tmp/card.figcraft
figcraft-cli info /tmp/card.figcraft          # independent read-back
figcraft-cli export /tmp/card.figcraft -o /tmp/card.png --node "Card" --scale 2
```

## Tools (18)

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `list_commands {filter?}` | ids, labels, menus, shortcuts, undoable, param docs |
| `run_command {command, params}` | any command (`align.left`, `layout.add`, `component.create`, `proto.*`, `inspect.*`…) |
| `batch {commands, label?}` | many commands, one undo step; `{"$step": n}` references an earlier id |
| `create_node {type, x?, y?, width?, height?, parent?, index?, name?, text?, path?, props?}` | frame, rectangle, ellipse, polygon, star, line, arrow, vector, text, section, component, slice |
| `set_properties {ids, props}` | `node.set` on layers; returns `{nodes:[…], ok:true}` |
| `inspect_document {depth?, allPages?}` | layer tree, pages, styles, selection, history; **depth 0 has no children** |
| `get_node {id, depth?}` | one layer, children to `depth` |
| `select {ids}` | replace selection (`[]` deselects) |
| `export {ids?, format, scale?/size?, path?, …}` | png/jpg/webp/svg/pdf/fig; without ids: selection, else page |
| `screenshot {ids?, scale?, maxSize?, window?}` | PNG of the design, or the app window when attached |
| `open_file {path, variables?}` / `save_file {path?}` | open `.figcraft/.json/.fig/.svg/image`; save as `.figcraft` |
| `undo` / `redo` | one command / batch / gesture per step |
| `pointer {kind, x, y, to?, steps?, tool?, shift?, alt?, cmd?}` | click/double/drag/down/move/up/hover in page coordinates; `to` is `[x, y]` |
| `key {key, shift?, alt?, cmd?}` | shortcut or key as if typed on the canvas |
| `type_text {text, id?}` | replace a text layer's characters, or type into the edit |
| `inspect_ui {}` | tool, canvas, panels, windows, status, timings (attached); **no `view`** — use `view.get` |

Resources: `figcraft://document`, `figcraft://commands` (+ `figcraft://node/{id}` and
`figcraft://command/{id}` templates). Prompts: `mobile_screen`,
`design_system`, `landing_page`, `prototype_flow`.

## Safest default workflow

1. **Probe first.** `inspect_document` for the current state; `list_commands {filter:"…"}`
   before guessing an id or parameter.
2. **Start from a template** when the task is a whole app/site:
   `run_command {command:"file.newFromTemplate", params:{template:"mobile-app"}}`, or create
   a blank document with `file.new` (this opens a **new tab**, it does not reset the old one).
3. **Build with `batch`** and `{"$step": n}` references — one undo step, all-or-nothing.
4. **Read back** each important layer (`get_node`) before styling further.
5. **Export/render to check pixels** (`export` PNG then look at it; `screenshot` for the page).
6. **Save a copy** with an explicit `.figcraft` path; confirm with `figcraft-cli info`.
7. **Only then** touch a user file, and never overwrite one without a copy in a test dir.

## Finding commands

`list_commands {filter:"auto layout"}` (the filter is a **literal, case-insensitive substring**:
`"autoLayout"` matches nothing). CLI: `figcraft-cli commands --filter "auto layout"` or
`--json`. Biggest namespaces: `text` 56, `view` 48, `vector` 40, `object` 28 (full table in
`references/commands.md`). Never guess a parameter — query it.

## Verify your work

- Numbers: `get_node`, `inspect_document`.
- Pixels: `export`/`screenshot` → `identify file.png` (`file`, `pdfinfo`, `pdftotext` for PDF).
- Saved files: `figcraft-cli info path --json`; a `.figcraft` is a zip (`unzip -l`).
- UI: `inspect_ui` (attached), `screenshot {window:true}`.

## Pitfalls (verified in 0.8.0 — details in `references/bugs-and-workarounds.md`)

- **`save_file` does not check the extension.** `save_file {path:"x.png"}` writes a `.figcraft`
  **zip** named `x.png` and reports success. Always end native saves in `.figcraft`.
- **`export` writes the format you ask for, not the one the path suggests.**
  `format:"png", path:"x.jpg"` writes PNG bytes into `x.jpg`; `file.export {format:"pdf",
  path:"x.png"}` writes a PDF named `x.png`.
- **`inspect.code` takes `language`, not `format`.** An unknown key is ignored and you silently
  get CSS.
- **`create_node` and `node.create` ignore unknown arguments**; `node.set`/`set_properties`
  reject unknown properties by name ("unknown properties: …"). Typos in props are therefore
  loud, typos in tool arguments are silent.
- **`opacity` outside 0–1 is rescaled, not rejected:** `2` → `0.02`, `-1` → `0`. Stay in 0–1.
- **Negative sizes clamp to 0** (`width:-50` → 0) with no warning.
- **`export` with no ids uses the selection**, so "nothing to export" or a one-layer export
  usually means something is still selected. `select.none` first for a whole page.
- **PDF:** one page per top-level frame only when exporting the page; with `ids` you get one page.
- **SVG outlines text by default**; pass `svgOutlineText:false` for real `<text>`.
- **`file.new` opens an additional tab**, and `open_file` on an already-open file returns
  `{opened:{index}}` with no summary.
- **`page.delete` takes its layers with it** (undoable). Sections go only on a page or in a
  section, not inside frames.
- **Attached mode on Wayland:** if the window is covered or minimised the compositor stops
  drawing it; UI work then waits and fails with "timed out waiting for the UI". A timed-out
  request was seen to wedge the control channel (even `initialize` hung) until the app was
  restarted — kill only a FigCraft you started, then relaunch.
- **`file.close` never prompts**: it errors on unsaved changes unless `{force:true}`.
- **`.fig` is best effort** (import and export); verify what came back.

## What was not tested

Live sessions/`figcraft-server`, plugins, comments/Dev Mode end-to-end, presentation player,
printing, the browser/WASM build, real Figma `.fig` files, Display P3, missing-font fallback,
i18n, accessibility, and documents beyond ~2,000 layers. Exact export checks:
`references/formats-and-roundtrip.md`.

## Reference files

`references/`: `commands.md` (ids + params by namespace), `recipes.md` (task recipes),
`mcp-and-control.md` (protocol, tools, control channel, coordinates, windows, confinement),
`cli.md`, `formats-and-roundtrip.md`, `bugs-and-workarounds.md`, `maintenance.md`.
`scripts/`: `probe.sh`, `dump-commands.sh`, `smoke-test.sh`.

## Maintenance

```sh
bash ~/.config/opencode/skills/figcraft/scripts/probe.sh          # versions, tools, counts
bash ~/.config/opencode/skills/figcraft/scripts/dump-commands.sh  # catalog snapshot + diff
bash ~/.config/opencode/skills/figcraft/scripts/smoke-test.sh     # headless end-to-end
node ~/.config/opencode/skills/creating-skills/scripts/check-skill.mjs \
  ~/.config/opencode/skills/figcraft
```

The snapshot above was verified on **2026-10-22 against 0.8.0**. Command ids, parameters,
counts and tool names can change between releases; confirm before relying on a detail.
