#1130 [Audit] Minor 21: Server key compared in plaintext (docs say hash), constant time

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-22 by PierrunoYT · updated 2026-10-22

Severity: Low
Category: Minor (doc/code mismatch, length oracle)
Location: apps/figcraft-server/src/store.rs:1416, :319-335; crates/collab/src/lib.rs:50-53; docs/server.md:460

Summary: The operator key is compared in plaintext via same_secret, while the docs say keys are compared against hashes.

Detail (from code):

  • store.rs:1416 (manage()): match same_secret(key, &self.key) {
  • same_secret (collab/src/lib.rs:50-53): 
    pub fn same_secret(a: &str, b: &str) -> bool {
    let (a, b) = (a.as_bytes(), b.as_bytes());
    a.len() == b.len() && a.iter().zip(b).fold(0u8, |acc, (x, y)| acc | (x ^ y)) == 0
}
  • self.key is the raw key read by load_key (store.rs:319-327); link/code/owner tokens do hash first (store.rs:634,806; codes.rs:74), but the operator key does not. Docs (server.md:460) claim "all are compared in constant time against hashes".

Impact: The comparison is constant-time (OR-fold over XOR) but short-circuits on length, letting an adversary probe the key's length; the docs overstate the hash guarantee for the operator key.

Suggested fix: Store a hash of the server key (like other secrets) and compare hashes; update the docs to match.

#1129 [Audit] Minor 20: Partial temp cleanup

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-22 by PierrunoYT · updated 2026-10-22

Severity: Low
Category: Minor (temp-file accumulation)
Location: apps/figcraft-server/src/store.rs:427-433, :733, :771, :981, :1059, :1330, :333; apps/figcraft-server/src/directory.rs:89

Summary: The startup cleanup covers only the four core per-file temp artifacts (plus the plugin index); usage.json.tmp, library-<version>.bin.tmp, blocked.json.tmp, reports.json.tmp and server.key.tmp are missed.

Detail (from code):

for name in [SNAPSHOT, LOG, META, LINKS] {
    let tmp = disk::temp_of(&path.join(name));
    if tmp.exists() { let _ = fs::remove_file(&tmp); }
}
  • Covered: per-file snapshot.bin.tmp, log.bin.tmp, meta.json.tmp, links.json.tmp and the plugin index.json.tmp (directory.rs:89).
  • Not covered: per-file usage.json.tmp (store.rs:1059 via write_json→write_atomic at 1330), per-file library-<version>.bin.tmp (store.rs:981), root blocked.json.tmp/reports.json.tmp (store.rs:733,771), and root server.key.tmp (store.rs:333). No orphaned-file scan exists.

Impact: After a crash mid-write, partial temp files accumulate indefinitely (disk waste, leftover plaintext data on disk).

Suggested fix: Extend the startup sweep to every write_atomic/write_json target and add an orphan scan.

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-22 by PierrunoYT · updated 2026-10-22

Severity: Low

#1126 [Audit] Minor 17: Bidi characters in names

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-22 by PierrunoYT · updated 2026-10-22

Severity: Low
Category: Minor (terminal spoofing)
Location: apps/figcraft-server/src/store.rs:293-295, :751; apps/figcraft-server/src/cli.rs:395, :414, :436-438

Summary: clean_name and report-reason filters strip only Cc control chars; bidi format chars (U+202E etc.) pass through to the operator's terminal.

Detail (from code):

  • store.rs:294: s.trim().chars().filter(|c| !c.is_control()).take(256).collect()
  • store.rs:751 (report reason): reason.trim().chars().map(|c| if c.is_control() { ' ' } else { c }).take(MAX_REASON).collect()
  • char::is_control() returns true only for General_Category Cc; U+202E (RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE) and other bidi format chars (category Cf) pass through. elide (cli.rs:436-438) only truncates by char count.

Impact: A malicious file/sender name can carry bidi overrides into the operator's terminal tables, enabling spoofed/visual-reordering display tricks in server logs and listings.

Suggested fix: Also filter bidi format chars (Cf) — e.g. strip U+202A–U+202E and other directional marks — in clean_name and report reasons.

#1125 [Audit] Minor 16: 32-bit font index overflow

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-22 by PierrunoYT · updated 2026-10-22

Severity: Low
Category: Minor (offset corruption / debug panic)
Location: crates/text/src/fontdb.rs:837-869 (index_bytes)

Summary: at + 4, at + 12, and at + 12 + 16 * t are unchecked usize additions that can wrap on 32-bit targets.

Detail (from code):

let Some(tables) = fill(&mut buf, at, 12).and_then(|()| be(&buf, at + 4, 2)) else { continue };
if fill(&mut buf, at + 12, 16 * tables).is_none() {
...
for rec in (0..tables).map(|t| at + 12 + 16 * t) {
  • at is a file-controlled u32 (from be(&buf, 12 + 4 * i, 4)); 16 * tables itself cannot overflow (tables is a u16, max 65535 → ~1.05M).
  • The helper closures fill/be use checked_add, so no out-of-bounds memory access results — the overflow corrupts the offset, not memory safety.

Impact: On 32-bit native targets, a crafted font file with a huge table offset wraps at + 12, causing the scan to read table-name data from the wrong offset (mis-indexed fonts) and, in debug builds, panic — turning untrusted font input into a crash.

Suggested fix: Use checked_add for the offset family and reject files whose offsets would overflow.

#1123 [Audit] Minor 14: Panic guard missing on wasm

maintainer labelshared · opened 2026-10-22 by PierrunoYT · updated 2026-10-22

Severity: Low
Category: Minor (safety net missing on web)
Location: crates/pathops/src/lib.rs:64-66; crates/pathops/Cargo.toml:118

Summary: The linesweeper catch_unwind guard does nothing on wasm32, where panics abort the instance.

Detail (from code):

// shortcut: no catch where panics abort (wasm32); drop this once a linesweeper release no longer panics there.
fn sweep<T>(f: impl FnOnce() -> Result<T, PathOpsError>) -> Result<T, PathOpsError> {
    std::panic::catch_unwind(std::panic::AssertUnwindSafe(f)).unwrap_or(Err(PathOpsError::BadInput))
}
  • No #[cfg] alternative exists; Cargo.toml:118 corroborates: // wasm32-unknown-unknown always aborts on panic, so panic = "abort" changes nothing there.

Impact: On wasm builds, rare near-degenerate path input that panics the linesweeper aborts the wasm instance instead of returning PathOpsError::BadInput — the intended safety net silently doesn't exist on the web target.

Suggested fix: Use catch_unwind only where it works (non-wasm), and on wasm keep the guard logic out of the panicking path or fix the upstream panic.

#1120 [Audit] Minor 11: Library-fetch thread can hang

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-22 by PierrunoYT · updated 2026-10-22

Severity: Low
Category: Minor (thread leak / hang)
Location: crates/collab-net/src/manage.rs:210-213

Summary: The close() helper reads until an error; a server that keeps the socket alive (e.g. repeating pings) pins the loop forever.

Detail (from code):

fn close(mut ws: Ws) {
    let _ = ws.close(None);
    while ws.read().is_ok() {}
}
  • close() is used by library/plugins one-shot fetches (manage.rs:170,195).
  • The read timeout set in connect (manage.rs:205, idle_timeout) bounds a silent server, but any server that keeps the socket alive (repeating pings/Pong, surfaced by tungstenite as Ok) makes read() return Ok forever.

Impact: close() never returns against a chatty/uncooperative server, so the library/plugins request thread leaks and hangs indefinitely — there is no deadline on the polite-close drain.

Suggested fix: Add a deadline to the close-drain loop (e.g. read_timeout on the socket, or a bounded number of reads).

depth < 64
    && match params {
        Value::Object(m) => m.iter().any(|(k, v)| (k == "pluginData" && own(v)) || writes_widget_data(v, depth + 1)),

Impact: Deeply nested pluginData payloads (depth 64–128) evade writes_widget_data, so the sandbox under-reports whether a plugin wrote widget data — a divergence between the check and what serde actually accepts.

Suggested fix: Raise the check depth to match serde's limit (128) or lower serde's limit to 64.

Suggested fix: Use read_capped with a sane limit on all caller-given path branches.

let mut reply = String::new();

  • reply is a plain String; BufReader::read_line appends until newline/EOF with no size limit.

#1110 [Audit] Minor 1: Control channel

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-22 by PierrunoYT · updated 2026-10-22

Severity: Low
Category: Minor (local availability DoS)
Location: apps/figcraft/src/control_server.rs:15-18, :52, :64-65

Summary: The local control channel has only 8 connection slots with a 60‑second idle timeout; a local peer can hold every slot and starve other local clients.

Detail (from code):

  • Constants (control_server.rs:15-18): 
    const MAX_CONNECTIONS: usize = 8;
const TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(60);
  • spawn_connection (line 52) rejects connections once workers.len() >= MAX_CONNECTIONS.
  • serve (lines 64-65) sets a read/write timeout of TIMEOUT — an idle timeout, so a peer sending a line every <60s holds its slot indefinitely.

Impact: A local process can occupy all 8 slots and keep them alive, blocking other local tools/agents (and the MCP --attach client) from the control channel — a local-only availability issue (8 slots × 60s is trivially exhaustible).

Suggested fix: Require an explicit per-connection deadline or per-peer quota; reduce idle timeout; or use a single multiplexed control channel.

#1106 [Audit] RND-11: unique_id is O(n^2) for repeated layer names (Low)

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-22 by PierrunoYT · updated 2026-10-22

Severity: Low
Category: DoS (CPU)
Location:

  • crates/svg/src/lib.rs:549-555 (unique_id)
    Summary: unique_id is O(n²) for repeated layer names.
    Status: Confirmed

Verified (from code):

fn unique_id(&mut self, name: &str) -> String {
    let base: String = name.chars().take(200).map(|c| if c.is_whitespace() || c.is_control() { '_' } else { c }).collect();
    let base = if base.is_empty() { "layer".to_string() } else { base };
    let id = (1..).map(|k| if k == 1 { base.clone() } else { format!("{base}_{k}") }).find(|i| !self.used_ids.contains(i)).unwrap_or(base);
    self.used_ids.insert(id.clone());
    id
}
  • For each new id the code scans k = 1,2,… until an unused suffix is found (used_ids is a HashSet, so contains is O(1)); N layers sharing a base name cost O(N²) membership checks.

Impact: Exporting documents with many same-named layers (e.g. 100k "Rectangle"s) is quadratic — noticeable export stall on large files.

Suggested fix: Keep a HashMap<String, usize> of next-suffix per base name and emit base_k directly.

fn binary(a: &BezPath, b: &BezPath, op: linesweeper::BinaryOp) -> Result<BezPath, PathOpsError> {
    if a.elements().is_empty() && b.elements().is_empty() { return Ok(BezPath::new()); }

    let contours = sweep(|| linesweeper::binary_op(&closed(a), &closed(b), ...))?;
  • Only emptiness and finiteness are checked; no element-count/bbox/area cap. boolean_ops folds arbitrarily many operands, each running the sweep on the accumulated result.

Impact: A document with huge or many boolean operands causes quadratic/high-memory sweep work and can peg CPU on interaction/export; sweep catches panics but not resource blow-up.

Suggested fix: Add caps (total elements per operand/accumulated, bbox area) returning PathOpsError::BadInput past the budget.

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-22 by PierrunoYT · updated 2026-10-22

Severity: Low

    Summary: A new file's directory entry is not fsynced before the publisher is answered.
    Status: Plausible

Verified (from code):

let written = fs::create_dir_all(&dir).map_err(...)
    .and_then(|()| disk::write_atomic(&dir.join(SNAPSHOT), &bytes)...)
    .and_then(|()| disk::write_atomic(&dir.join(LOG), ...)...)
    .and_then(|()| write_json(&dir.join(LINKS), ...))
    .and_then(|()| write_json(&dir.join(META), &meta));
  • create_dir_all doesn't fsync the parent (<root>/files); write_atomic syncs each temp file and the file's own folder, never the directory that records the new folder's entry (sync_dir is a no-op on Windows).

Impact: After power loss/panic the newly published file may disappear despite all its writes being synced — an atomicity/durability gap.

Suggested fix: After create_dir_all(&dir), fsync the parent (disk::sync_dir(Some(&self.root.join(FILES)))).

Source: FigCraft security & robustness audit (rev 9ec80bf2, 2026-10-22) - AUDIT.md, verified against the workspace code..

#1087 [Audit] COL-10: Message size limit raised to full size before token check (Low)

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-22 by PierrunoYT · updated 2026-10-22

Severity: Low
Category: DoS (pre-auth)
Location:

  • crates/collab-net/src/hub.rs:949-952 (raise read cap)
  • crates/collab-net/src/hub.rs:1352 (join/backend.admit)
    Summary: Message size limit is raised to the full size before the token is checked.
    Status: Confirmed

Verified (from code):

ws.set_config(|c| *c = config(max));        // max = limits.max_client_message (64MiB)
let opened = sock.try_clone().is_ok_and(|s| hub.send(HubIn::Open { ... }).is_ok());
if opened && ws.get_ref().set_read_timeout(Some(idle)).is_ok() {
    read_loop(&mut ws, conn, hub, limits, max, &shared.in_flight, &end);
  • The read cap is raised from max_hello (64KiB) to max_client_message (64MiB) before the hub processes HubIn::Open, which is where join() runs backend.admit(...) (line 1352) — the token check.

Impact: An unauthenticated connection can push messages up to 64MiB before/without any token validation — multi-MiB per-message allocations upstream of rejection.

Suggested fix: Keep the read cap at max_hello until the hello/token is admitted; only then raise it to max_client_message.

Source: FigCraft security & robustness audit (rev 9ec80bf2, 2026-10-22) - AUDIT.md, verified against the workspace code..

#1000 node.create / node.set: apply a paint style or bind a variable in props

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-21 by kkilchrist · updated 2026-10-21

Summary

Creating a themed layer takes extra steps: create it with a hex colour, then style.apply or variable.bind it in a separate call or a second pass. Building a design system screen, an agent ends up creating everything in hex and then running selection.colors → selection.applyColorStyle over the result to tokenise it (that pass worked well, binding about 400 colour slots in one batch, but it's a workaround).

Proposal

Accept styles and variables directly in props for node.create / node.set:

{"command":"node.create","params":{"type":"text","text":"Today","props":{
  "fillStyle":"Theme/ink",
  "strokeStyle":"Theme/line"}}}
{"command":"node.set","params":{"ids":[12],"props":{"fill":{"$var":"Macros Theme/surface"}}}}

Either style names or ids, and variables by name or id. This mirrors how fontFamily already takes a name.

Environment

figcraft-cli 0.8.0 (macOS universal), macOS 27.2.

Found by Claude (Opus 5.5) in Claude Code while building about 80 phone screens through the FigCraft MCP server.

#936 Chinese UI font looks too thin / faint in light mode (11px, thin strokes)

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-20 by yelintong · updated 2026-10-20

Symptom

In light mode, the Chinese (and other CJK) text in the UI looks noticeably faint / thin — the strokes are too light and the text reads as washed-out and airy. The exact same CJK font looks far more solid in dark mode. Affects body text, buttons and sidebar labels.

Environment

  • Theme: light (Tokens::light, text color #1E1E1E; contrast itself already meets WCAG AA).
  • Platform: Windows (system font scan). Most default setups do not have misans_dir / CRAFT_FONTS_DIR.

Investigation (points to code)

  • crates/ui-egui/src/theme.rs → install_fonts():
    • Body / Button font sizes are only 11px, Small 10px (set in apply_with for TextStyle::Body / Button).
    • There is a misans_dir() path (theme.rs:304–319) that loads MiSans Medium for the body chrome, with the comment "Medium for the body chrome so the UI doesn't read as too thin at 11px" (theme.rs:307). This MiSans path is an experimental test, not the shipped default — it is absent in most setups, so the UI falls back to a system CJK face.
    • The default fallback is a system CJK font (crates/ui-egui/src/cjk.rs's CHINESE list: Noto Sans CJK SC / Microsoft YaHei UI / PingFang SC …), which renders thin at 11px.
    • Note: even the MiSans Medium test still looked faint, and the default (non-MiSans) font is even fainter — so the problem is worst for users on the default setup, and weight alone is not a complete fix.
  • Tokens::light() uses text = #1E1E1E — contrast is fine, so "faint" is a stroke-weight / font-size problem, not a foreground-color-contrast problem.

Possible causes

  1. On a light background, thin CJK strokes read as more "faint" than on a dark background (anti-aliasing is more visible on low-contrast edges).
  2. The system fallback CJK face is a Regular / thin weight, while Inter uses inter-semibold for headings and body CJK has no medium-weight fallback.
  3. 11px is simply small for CJK; at the same size Latin letters stay more legible than hanzi.

Suggested directions

  • Give the default CJK fallback a Medium / heavier weight, or bump the Chinese UI font size slightly (e.g. +1px) in install_fonts.
  • Consider a one-off gamma / stroke tweak for CJK in light mode (egui FontTweak).

#555 Feature Request: Binding Actions to Button/Key Events

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-15 by Papermanzero · updated 2026-10-15

There is already a discussion at Figma concerning Button Events.

https://forum.figma.com/suggest-a-feature-11/key-press-or-key-down-trigger-should-exist-40810

There should be the functionality to control the UI via keyboard or button (controller) events
The events which are required are:

Press (Time)
Description for the event: A key/button is pressed for a certain time -
By default, the event triggers an action immediately if a key/button is pressed. The time can be overwritten with a time parameter (for instance 0,5 seconds). That means if a key/button is pressed for 0,5 seconds it triggers an action.

Release (Time)
Description for the event: A key/button is released after a certain time -
By default, the event triggers an action immediately if a key/button is released. The time can be overwritten with a time parameter (for instance 0,5 seconds). That means if a key/button is released after 0,5 seconds it triggers an action.

With those two actions you can combine various key/button combinations. For instance press the “A” key for one second opens a menu. If you release “A” key after one second the menu closes.

1 comment
Hamza0101 · 2026-10-18

Reproduced, and it is not only a display issue — the same gap is in the exported PNG.

Built four 20×20 squares abutting at (20, 20) with the same fill, through figcraft-cli, and read the pixels back:

render size lightest interior pixel
--scale 1 40×40 none — solid
--scale 2.5 100×100 none — solid
--scale 1.37 55×55 (27, 27) r=77
--scale 0.73 30×30 (14, 14) r=77

r=77 on a #000000 fill over white, at exactly the point where the four squares meet. The script:

figcraft-cli run abut.json --out abut.figcraft   # four rects at (0,0) (20,0) (0,20) (20,20), 20×20, #000000
figcraft-cli render abut.figcraft -o s137.png --scale 1.37

So it reproduces whenever the shared edge does not land on a pixel boundary, and disappears when it does — which is why it comes and goes with zoom, and why zooming further makes it vanish.

What it looks like. Each shape is rasterised and composited on its own, so along a shared edge each covers about half the pixel: two 50 % blacks composited over white give about 75 %, not 100 %, and the remaining quarter shows through as a hairline. 77/255 is close to that quarter. Nothing is wrong with the geometry — the squares really do abut — so no amount of zooming reveals a gap in the document.

That makes it a conflation artifact rather than a rounding error in the coordinates, and the fixes are architectural rather than local: accumulate coverage across shapes before compositing, or merge touching same-paint shapes into one path before filling. Both are renderer-wide decisions with performance and correctness trade-offs well past a drive-by patch, so I am leaving the choice to you rather than sending one.

Two things worth noting for triage: the export is affected, not just the canvas, so a file exported for print or handoff carries the seams; and a fixture is cheap to assert on — render abutting same-fill rects at a fractional scale and no interior pixel should differ from the fill — if you want a regression test pinned before the fix.

Currently, online collaboration in FigCraft works by either uploading the document to the public server (collab.craftapps.dev)—where the file is stored unencrypted—or by manually provisioning and hosting a figcraft-server instance on a VPS with TLS/domain configuration.

I would like to propose adding support for Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) (or ephemeral local tunneling) so users can host live collaboration sessions directly from their own machine without uploading their files to a third-party server or configuring port forwarding.

Motivation & Benefits

  1. True Local-First Privacy: FigCraft emphasizes local files, offline capability, and privacy. Hosting the session directly from the host's machine via a tunnel means sensitive .figcraft files never have to be stored at rest on collab.craftapps.dev. When the host ends the session, the tunnel closes and the data remains strictly on their disk.
  2. Zero-Config Self-Hosting: Setting up figcraft-server on a public server requires a VPS, domain, and TLS certs (wss://). Cloudflare Quick Tunnels (cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:<port>) require no account, no port forwarding, and automatically provision a public https:// / wss:// URL (*.trycloudflare.com) with full WebSocket support.
  3. Reduced Infrastructure Cost for Maintainers: Offloading ad-hoc collaboration sessions to peer-hosted local servers via Cloudflare Tunnels reduces bandwidth and storage load on collab.craftapps.dev.

Proposed Workflow / Implementation Ideas

There are two stages this could be implemented in:

Phase 1: Custom Server URL in the UI + Documentation (Low Effort)

  • Allow users to easily specify a custom server URL in the Share -> Online modal at runtime (note: README.md mentions the default server is currently a build-time setting).
  • Add a section in docs/server.md showing how a user can run figcraft-server locally and expose it in one command: 
    # Terminal 1: Run local server
figcraft-server --bind 127.0.0.1:8080

# Terminal 2: Expose via Cloudflare Quick Tunnel
cloudflared tunnel --url [http://127.0.0.1:8080](http://127.0.0.1:8080)

#473 Add Dart/Flutter Code Support in Dev Mode

maintainer label · opened 2026-10-15 by KasamZB · updated 2026-10-15

It would be great to have Dart and Flutter code support in Dev Mode, similar to how Figma provides code inspection and developer handoff capabilities.

As a Flutter developer, I would like to inspect design elements in FigCraft and view their corresponding Dart/Flutter code directly in Dev Mode. This would make it much easier to translate designs into Flutter applications without manually recreating every UI element.

Proposed Features

Dart/Flutter Code Generation: Generate Flutter-compatible Dart code for selected design elements, components, and complete screens.

Code Inspection: Display relevant Dart code when selecting a layer or component, similar to the existing code inspection experience in Figma Dev Mode.

Property Mapping: Show corresponding Flutter properties for dimensions, padding, margins, alignment, colours, typography, borders, corner radius, and other styling attributes.

Widget Structure: Represent design elements using appropriate Flutter widgets, such as Container, Row, Column, Stack, Text, and Image.

Copy Code: Allow developers to copy the generated Dart code directly for use in their Flutter projects.

Reusable Components: Where possible, generate reusable Flutter widgets for components and repeated design elements.

Why Is This Important?

Flutter is widely used for cross-platform mobile application development. Native Dart/Flutter support would make FigCraft more useful for Flutter developers and teams looking for an open-source alternative to Figma.

Currently, developers need to manually interpret design properties and convert them into Flutter widgets. Built-in Dart code inspection and generation could significantly reduce implementation time, improve design-to-code accuracy, and simplify collaboration between designers and Flutter developers.

Expected Outcome

A dedicated Dart/Flutter option in Dev Mode, alongside other supported code formats, that allows developers to inspect design properties and obtain clean, editable Flutter code directly from their designs.

This feature would make FigCraft an even stronger alternative to Figma for teams building applications with Flutter.

Thank you for building and maintaining this open-source project!

#357 CraftHub: closing gap #2 (collaboration without accounts) — a decision brief for the administrators

classified in this triage · opened 2026-10-14 by hasan-sdaif · updated 2026-10-16

Triage note: Decision brief proposing CraftHub (accounts, teams, permissions) to close gap #2. Owner decision; relates to #742 and #609.

The one paragraph

The family is fourteen world-class apps, each clean, independent and privacy-complete — and today a set of individual tools: collaborating means emailing files, selling means no marketplace exists, and anyone without a powerful machine (or unwilling to install) is excluded entirely. Your own docs record the gap: collab-protocol.md names its unexecuted step six as "Accounts: people signing in, per-person permissions, teams and projects" — the structure is ready; the missing layer is accounts, teams and permissions above it. docs/gaps.md ranks "sync and sharing preview, without accounts" as gap #2, a beta blocker.

CraftHub is that layer — built over the protocol this repository already proved, with literal backwards compatibility (a v2 client keeps working against a v3 server with its full current behaviour; new messages ride feature words, exactly how v2 itself grew four times).

What is delivered today

  • hasan-sdaif/crafthub — the reference implementation, proposed for adoption: the generalized collaboration core (craft-collab, ported from figcraft-collab with its property tests: fractional indexing, server-ordered LWW with refusal fixes, per-user undo, join codes, the RGA text property, the three-way merge, the per-seed convergence simulator), protocol v3 shapes, identity/authz (64 capabilities × 8 roles, tested cell by cell), teams, review, comments, notifications, assets, BYO-cloud storage, the marketplace domain (integer money, a chained double-entry ledger, offline-verifiable license certificates), the payments discipline (PayPal P0 + Stripe P0, hosted checkout only, PCI SAQ-A), the i18n engine with Arabic's six plural categories, the MCP tool catalog, the server binary with the full TOML configuration, and the figcraft/wordcraft reference adapters. CI runs the family gate on GitHub Actions. An honest ROADMAP tracks M0-M15 with err-low grades.
  • storytold/craft-libs PR #128 — craft-collab published as the shared library (the specification's one sanctioned exception to "repos don't share code"), so the apps consume it by git reference exactly as they consume craft-print.
  • hasan-sdaif/craftmarket — the public web platform's reference scaffold (browse, buy, sell, download with zero installs), with its decision memo.

The two decisions asked of the administrators

  1. Adopt craftmarket (the public web platform, spec §22): the memo is delivered in both repos with an explicit yes/no/defer question. Rejecting breaks nothing — everything in crafthub works without it.
  2. Choose the sustainability stance (spec §23): a menu of off-by-default models (support donations, adjustable commission, contributor revenue share, a bounty economy that makes programmers compete to develop the project). The recommendation: support-only at launch. Changing stance later is configuration, not a rebuild.

Full brief: docs/proposals/crafthub-brief.md — written to be read alone in ten minutes, with the hard questions answered honestly (does "no accounts" break? no — accounts are purely optional, link sharing keeps working; do we become data hostages? no — bring-your-own-cloud; does money corrupt the culture? every financial layer sits behind kill switches and donations open zero capabilities, enforced by CI).

The compatibility promise (the part this repository cares about most)

  • The v2 protocol is preserved verbatim: figcraft://join?... links, share links, join codes, open hosting, team libraries, the plugin folder — all keep working against a CraftHub server.
  • The migration tool imports a figcraft-server data directory with no loss and a week of parallel running (spec §18.10).
  • figcraft migrates to craft-collab in its own repository, behind a feature flag, with its LAN hosting untouched (M9).

Credits

Reference implementation prepared by @hasan-sdaif against the CraftHub specification (§0-§24, 400 features, milestones M0-M15). Arabic-locale contributor of the family (vectorcraft's Craft AI local assistant PR #2010, the Arabic interface translations across the apps) — building in the family's own style: honest ROADMAPs, clean-room, MIT OR Apache-2.0, the craftrules constitution.

#248 Feature request: Figma plugins

classified in this triage · opened 2026-10-14 by googlyeyes47 · updated 2026-10-14

Triage note: Run existing Figma JS plugins. Large and raises clean-room concerns (the plugin API surface); consider closing as out of scope or tracking as a long-term idea.

I know this is probably going to have to wait until later, however, it would be great if this could be made to run figma plugins as well somehow.

Here's what an AI proposed to do to be able to implement this:

Summary & Motivation

Currently, docs/target-app-parity.md notes that FigCraft supports its own sandboxed WebAssembly plugins (Plugins and widgets: ~35%), while existing Figma plugins written in JavaScript do not run.

Because the Figma ecosystem relies heavily on community plugins (icon packs, token exporters, content generators, batch renamers, accessibility checkers), adding a clean-room Figma JS Plugin Compatibility Layer would dramatically accelerate FigCraft's "Ready for real work" score without violating FigCraft's core architectural rules (pure Rust/WASM, zero telemetry, offline-first, no GPL code, and strict engine/UI crate layering).

Below is a phased developer/agent implementation guide designed around FigCraft's existing Command Registry and WASM Sandbox so this can be implemented incrementally.

Architectural Fit (Honoring AGENTS.md)

Figma plugins follow a strict dual-process architecture invented for security—which maps directly onto FigCraft's existing architecture:

  1. Main Thread (Sandbox): Runs standard ES2020 JavaScript with zero DOM/network access and interacts with the document strictly through the global figma.* object (figma.createFrame(), figma.currentPage.selection, etc.).
  2. UI Thread (ui.html): Optional HTML/JS UI that communicates with the Main Thread strictly via asynchronous JSON messages (figma.ui.postMessage() / parent.postMessage()).

Because FigCraft already routes every scene-graph mutation through a central Command Registry and already supports WASM plugin sandboxes, we do not need Electron or V8 to run the vast majority of Figma plugins.

Phased Implementation Guide for Developers / Agents

Phase 1: Manifest Parser & Headless figma.* Runtime (QuickJS or Boa)

Goal: Run 100% of "headless" / menu-command Figma plugins (relaunchButtons, batch tools, auto-formatters, node generators) with zero UI changes.

  1. Manifest Loader (manifest.json):

    • Add a loader in the plugin crate that parses standard Figma plugin manifest.json files (name, id, api, main, ui, parameters, menu, networkAccess).
    • Map manifest.menu items directly into FigCraft's Plugins menu and Command Palette.

  2. Pure-Rust / WASM JS Engine Integration:

    • Use boa_engine (100% pure Rust ECMAScript engine, MIT/Apache-2.0) or rquickjs (or compile QuickJS to a .wasm host module inside FigCraft's existing WASM plugin runner).
    • Advantage of boa_engine: Compiles natively on Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD, and wasm32-unknown-unknown (for the FigCraft browser build) with zero C toolchain dependencies.

  3. Global figma Object Bridge -> FigCraft Command Registry:

    • Inject a global figma object into the JS context before evaluating manifest.main (code.js).
    • Implement a proxy/handle map between FigCraft's internal Node IDs and JS SceneNode proxy objects:
      • Lifecycle: figma.closePlugin(message?), figma.notify(message, options?)
      • Document & Selection: figma.root, figma.currentPage, figma.currentPage.selection (getter/setter), figma.getNodeById(id)
      • Node Constructors: figma.createFrame(), figma.createRectangle(), figma.createText(), figma.createVector(), figma.createComponent(), figma.group(), figma.flatten()
      • Node Properties: Map getters/setters (x, y, width, height, fills, strokes, opacity, layoutMode, itemSpacing, padding*, characters) directly to FigCraft's scene graph and command history so a single plugin run commits as one atomic undo step.
      • Storage & Fonts: figma.clientStorage.getAsync/setAsync (backed by a local JSON file in the user's FigCraft config dir) and figma.loadFontAsync() (mapped to craft-fonts / FigCraft's text engine).

Phase 2: Bridging figma.ui Without Bloating the Binary

Goal: Support interactive plugins that call figma.showUI(__html__, options).

Most Figma plugins only use ui.html for a handful of text inputs, dropdowns, color pickers, and a "Run / Apply" button, passing a JSON payload via parent.postMessage({ pluginMessage: ... }, '*'). We can support this in two tiers:

Tier A: Lightweight Native egui HTML/Form Translator (Zero WebView Dependency)

  • Parse simple ui.html trees (or provide an automatic DOM-shim inside boa_engine) that intercepts <input>, <select>, <button>, and <textarea> elements and renders them natively inside an egui::Window panel.
  • Wire parent.postMessage({ pluginMessage }) to the main JS context's figma.ui.onmessage callback, and figma.ui.postMessage() to the UI context's window.onmessage.

Tier B: Optional OS WebView Bridge (wry) for Complex React/Canvas Plugin UIs

  • Behind an optional Cargo feature flag (e.g., webview-plugins), spawn an OS-native webview window (wry uses WebView2 on Windows, WebKit on macOS/Linux—adding ~0 MB of browser binary bloat).
  • Inject a tiny 15-line preload script into the WebView that intercepts window.parent.postMessage and forwards the JSON payload over an IPC channel to FigCraft's figma.ui.onmessage handler.
  • Enforce manifest.json's networkAccess.allowedDomains via Content-Security-Policy (CSP) headers so plugins remain private and offline-by-default unless explicitly permitted by the user.

Phase 3: Widget & Variables API Extensions

  • Variables & Styles: Wire figma.variables.getLocalVariables(), getLocalVariableCollections(), and createVariable() to FigCraft's existing Design Tokens / Variables engine.
  • Export: Wire node.exportAsync({ format: 'SVG' | 'PNG' | 'JPG' | 'PDF' }) to FigCraft's native export pipeline.

Suggested Verification & Test Harness (scorecard / CI)

To fit FigCraft's automated testing workflow:

  1. Create examples/figma-plugins/ containing 3 clean-room reference plugins constructed from Figma's public plugin typings (@figma/plugin-typings, MIT licensed):
    • 01-create-grid: Headless plugin using figma.createFrame(), layoutMode = "HORIZONTAL", fills, and figma.closePlugin().
    • 02-batch-rename: Selection-mutating plugin reading and writing figma.currentPage.selection[i].name.
    • 03-ui-message-roundtrip: Tests figma.showUI() + figma.ui.postMessage() <-> figma.ui.onmessage state updates.
  2. Add an integration test asserting that executing a plugin records a single undoable transaction in the Engine Command History.

Let me know what you think, if this would be possible later on or not.
